Yajñamūrti
(‘personified sacrifice’)
------------------------------------------
Some of the branches of the वेदस् like the Taittirīya Saṁhitā (

.3) identify विष्णु with यज्ञ or Vedic sacrifice. This यज्ञमूर्ति or Yajñapuruṣa is described as having three heads, three legs, seven hands and four horns. His body is red in colour and wears a वनमाला (garland of wild flowers). Apart from exhibiting the postures of protection and bestowal of boons (abhaya and varada mudrās) he holds several implements of sacrifice like the sruk and sruva (ladles).
Obviously this is a symbolic representation of a sacrifice.

yājyā
(‘that which is to be sacrificed’)
------------------------------------------
This is the technical name of a formula of consecration. It is a verse from the Ṛgveda chanted by the होतृ priest while a libation of आज्य (clarified butter) is offered by the अध्वर्यु priest. Before the recital begins, the अध्वर्यु gives directions to the होतृ with such statements as ‘samiddho yaja’ (‘Recite the याज्या verse for the deity Samidhaḥ’). Then the होतृ begins to chant the appropriate याज्या formula loudly, preceded by the invocation ‘ye yajāmahe’ and followed by ‘vauṣaṭ’.
The yājyās occur in prayājas and anuyājas.
See ANUYĀJA.

Yājñavalkya Smṛti
------------------------------------------
This is a well-known स्मृति belonging to the classical dharmaśāstra literature.
It is said to be a composition of the famous sage याज्ञवल्क्य, the promulgator of the Śukla यजुर्वेद Saṁhitā. Its style and ideas seem to be close to this Veda. The present edition as available now was probably finalised by A.
, though the original might be placed between 100 B. C. and A.

.
It has 1010 verses in the classical anuṣṭubh meter and has five standard commentaries by अपरार्क (A.
), Mitramiśra (17th century A. D.), शूलपाणि (circa A.
), विज्ञानेश्वर (circa A.
) and विश्वरूप (A.

).
It appears like a beautiful summary of the Manusmṛti.
Its contents may be briefly described as follows:

First Kāṇḍa
Fourteen विद्यास् or sources of know-ledge like the वेदस् and वेदाङ्गस्; expounders of धर्म; the sixteen सṁस्कारस्; the four āśramas; the eight forms of मर्रिअगे; on eating māṁsa or flesh; on दान or giving gifts; śrāddha and its varieties; some शान्तिस् or propitiatory rites; the नवग्रहस् or nine प्लनेत्स्; राजधर्म or duties of a king; fate and human effort; weights and measures.

Second Kāṇḍa
On the administration of justice; debts, interest and repayment; पर्तितिओन् of property; boundary disputes; on sale of property; गम्ब्लिन्ग्; crimes and punishment.

Third Kāṇḍa
On च्रेमतिओन् and बुरिअल्; after-death rites; āpaddharma or rules of conduct in distress; on वानप्रस्थ and सṁन्यास; human physiology; on आत्मज्ञान; yogins and मोक्ष (liberation); on hells; sins and expiations; yamas and niyamas; eulogy studying this work.

Yājñavalkya
------------------------------------------
Yājñavalkya was one of the wisest and the most illustrious among the Vedic sages. He was the son of the sage Brahmarāta and a nephew as also a disciple of वैशम्पायन. Once he incurred the wrath of his गुरु and was expelled by him, after surrendering the Veda (Yajurveda) to him. Later he pleased सूर्य (the Sun-god) and got a new Veda, which came to be known as the Śukla Yajurveda or Vājasaneyī Saṁhitā. (See YAJURVEDA for details.)
YājñavalkyaIn the scholarly debates on ब्रह्मन् arranged by the king जनक Vaideha, he emerged as the best and the most brilliant of all the scholarly ṛṣis (vide Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3rd Chapter).
He taught spiritual wisdom to his first wife मैत्रेयी who was a seeker of truth. His second wife कात्यायनी was not interested in it.
Two more works are attributed to him: Yogayājñavalkya and Yājñavalkya Smṛti.

yajñacakra
(‘the cycle of sacrifice’)
------------------------------------------
This is a special concept given by the Bhagavadgītā (3.10-16).
In the beginning God created the human beings, the gods in हेअवेन् as also yajña—the system of sacrifice and worship—as the link between them. The human beings were advised to worship the gods through यज्ञ; and, the gods would respond by giving them what they want or need to lead a happy life. It is by such mutual help and co-operation that both can be satisfied.
This is then followed by a description of how the whole च्रेअतिओन् is sustained by an interlinking of various factors, as follows: Living beings are produced by ड़ोओद्. ड़ोओद् is produced by rains. Rains are induced by the unseen but positive result of yajñas performed by the human beings. यज्ञ is brought about by the physical and ritual activity of the priests as also the performer of the sacrifice. The basis for the sacrificial system is the Veda. And, the Veda has emerged out of अक्षर or परमात्मन्, the Supreme God.
This in sum is the jagat-चक्र or यज्ञचक्र, since the Veda is primarily concerned with यज्ञ or sacrifice.

(‘sacrifice’)
------------------------------------------

Yajñavarāha
(‘[Vedic] sacrifice as the Boar [incarnation]’)
------------------------------------------
The Varāha or Boar-इन्चर्नतिओन् is the third in the series of ten incarnations (See DAŚĀVATĀRAS.) Sometimes, this form is associated with the origin of yajñas or वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् in all their details.
The Pāñcarātra texts like the Sātvata Saṁhitā (12.44.49) include यज्ञवराह among the 38 vibhāvatāras (glorious manifestations) of विष्णु.
This representation is highly symbolical. The legs of यज्ञवराह represent the four वेदस्, and the tusk the sacrificial altar. The face stands for all sacrifices, the tongue for fire and the hair for the sacred दर्भ grass. The two eyes symbolise day and night. The snout denotes all the offerings and oblations whereas the grunt stands for the सामन् (vide Viṣṇupurāṇa

-34).
Such descriptions are found in other texts like the Īśvarasaṁhitā (24.238-243) also.

yajñopavīta
(what is worn [during a] sacrifice’)
------------------------------------------
See UPANAYANA.

Yajñāyajñīya
------------------------------------------
A स्तोत्र is a Vedic chant composed of verses mainly taken from the Ṛgveda. It is generally chanted in ritual service. The यज्ञायज्ञीय is the name of a स्तोत्र chanted as a सामन् (set to Sāmavedic notes) in the tṛtīyasavana or the third pressing of the सोम juice in the अग्निष्टोम sacrifice (vide आपस्तम्ब Śrautasūtras 13.15.3). The उद्गातृ begins the chant. All, including the onlookers, can join in the chanting if they know it. However, they are expected to cover their heads and ears during chanting.

Yajurveda
------------------------------------------
The Yajurveda is the second of the four वेदस्, the basic scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म्. It is said to have emerged out of the southern face of ब्रह्मा, the creator. It is also called Adhvaryuveda, since its main use is in the performance of the वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् wherein the अध्वर्यु is the chief priest under whose direct guidance the entire sacrifice is performed. Its mantras are called yajus which are in prose.
Since the ancient times, it has been available in two main streams, the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda and the Śukla Yajurveda.
The popular legend that describes how this came about runs as follows: The sage वैशम्पायन, to whom वेदव्यास had imparted the Yajurveda, once incurred the sin of ब्रह्महत्या (the sin of killing a ब्राह्मण) due to a serious but technical lapse. Being too old and decrepit to perform the prescribed expiation, he asked his disciples to do it on his behalf which was permitted by the relevant scriptures. याज्ञवल्क्य, his best disciple, probably due to the pride of his learning, offered to do it all by himself thereby slighting the other disciples. Angered by this behaviour of his, वैशम्पायन ordered him to give back the Veda he had taught and quit.
Yājñavalkya then ‘vomitted’ the Veda which was black or dark in colour, and left. The other disciples took the form of tittiri birds (partridges) and consumed it. Since it was dark in colour, it came to be known as Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda (kṛṣṇa = dark, black). Since the tittiri birds consumed it, it was also called Taittirīya Saṁhitā.
Yājñavalkya later worshipped the Sun-god and got another version of the same Veda from him, who taught it assuming the form of a horse. Hence this branch came to be known as Śukla Yajurveda (śukla = white, bright) and Vājasaneyī Saṁhitā (vāji = horse).
Obviously this legend is highly symbolical which has to be unravelled carefully.
The following is one plausible explanation: याज्ञवल्क्य being the most brilliant of all the students of Vaiśam-pāyana, had mastered the whole of the Yajurveda. He was now forced to teach it to the other disciples. To the extent he taught it to them and to the extent they learnt it, that part of the Veda slipped out of his memory due to the curse of his गुरु. After thus losing it, he had to regain it—maybe in another form—by his own तपस् or austerities in which he succeeded. He pleased God through meditation on the Sun-form and got it.
The sage Tittiri was an important teacher of this Veda. He was a disciple coming in the great tradition of the Vedic teachers व्यास and वैशम्पायन. Hence this Veda got the name Taittirīya Saṁhitā. Similarly, since याज्ञवल्क्य was the son of ‘Vājaseni’ (‘one who was famous for giving the gift of vājas or ड़ोओद्’) Devarāta, his Veda came to be known as Vājasaneyī Saṁhitā. This is another explanation.
Normally, a Vedic Saṁhitā consists of only metrical compositions whereas the ब्राह्मणस् are in prose. Since the Veda taught by वैशम्पायन contained a mixture of these—which is rather unusual—it might have been called Kṛṣṇa (dark, not pure). The other Veda comprising of only the metrical compositions, might have got the title Śukla (white, pure).
Some scholars feel that the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda is the more ancient of the two.
As in the case of the other three वेदस्, the Yajurveda also has several branches. They are listed as 101 or 86. However only 5 Saṁhitās are available now. They are:
Taittirīya Saṁhitā
Maitrāyaṇīya Saṁhitā
Kāṭhaka Saṁhitā
Kapisthala-Kāṭhaka Saṁhitā
Vājasaneyī Saṁhitā
The first four belong to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. Out of these, the fourth has not been recovered fully.
The Vājasaneyī Saṁhitā is the only Saṁhitā of the Śukla Yajurveda and has two recensions: the Kāṇva and the Mādhyandina. Though 13 more have been mentioned, none of them is available now.
The commentators on the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda are: Kuṇḍina, Bhavasvāmin, Guhadeva, Bhaṭṭabhāskara, Kṣura, सायण, Veṅkateśa, Bālakṛṣṇa, हरदत्त and शत्रुघ्न.
The following are the commentators on the Śukla Yajurveda:
On the Kāṇvaśākhā: सायण, आनन्द-bodha, Anantācārya, Kālanātha, Murārimiśra, हलायुध, आदित्य-दर्शन, Devapāla and Somānanda-पुत्र.
On the Mādhyandinaśākhā: शौनक, Harisvāmin, Uraṭa, Gauradhara and महीधर.
As is well-known, each Veda has its own ब्राह्मणस्, आरण्यकस् and उपनिषद्स्.
The Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda has only one ब्राह्मण and one Āraṇyaka. They are: Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa and Taittirīya Āraṇyaka.
The उपनिषद्स् of this Veda are: the Taittirīya, the Kaṭha and the Śvetāśvatara.
Coming to the Śukla Yajurveda, the only ब्राह्मण available now is the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa. This too is in two recensions, the Kāṇva and the Mādhyandina.
The pūrvabhāga or first part of the 14th kāṇḍa (section) of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa is the Āraṇyaka of the Śukla Yajurveda. The last part of this ब्राह्मण is the well-known Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. The Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad also belongs to this Veda and forms the last chapter of the Saṁhitā.
(See under the respective titles for more details.)
The language of this Veda is not very different from that of the Ṛgveda. It describes in detail the performance of various वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् like Darśapūrṇa-māsa, अश्वमेध, राजसूय, Sautrāmaṇi, वाजपेय as also several Somayāgas.
Most of the gods of the Ṛgveda are found here also. Whereas some like रुद्र have become more important, others like उषस् have lost their prominence.
The society reflected through this Veda is similar to that of the Ṛgveda. The वर्ण system had been firmly established.
The philosophy of the Yajurveda is same as the one reflected in its उपनिषद्स्. The element of devotion to God is also an important factor to be noted.
